passages.title: All creation glorifies its all-knowing Creator
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat open the sūrah by placing you inside a universe that is already glorifying its Creator — and then telling you Who owns it, Who made you, and how completely He sees you. What holds them together is a single movement: from the glorification offered by all creation (ayah 1), to the making of *you* in particular and the parting of ways that follows (ayah 2), to the making of the heavens and earth with truth and the shaping of your own form (ayah 3), and finally to a knowledge that reaches into the chest itself (ayah 4). The passage begins with everything in the heavens and the earth, and ends with what you conceal.

## Where the sūrah opens

Ibn Kathir opens his comment by noting that this is **the last sūrah among al-Musabbiḥāt**, and recalls a point he has made before in that connection: **all creatures praise the glory of Allah, their Creator and Owner.** So the opening line is not a poetic flourish. It is a statement about reality: whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah.

Notice the scope the ayah gives itself — *whatever* is in the heavens and *whatever* is on the earth. Ibn Kathir's summary matches that breadth exactly: **all creatures.** Not only the angels, not only the believers. And notice that the translation offered here supplies the word "constantly" — this glorification is presented as the standing condition of creation, not an episode in it.

## Ayah 1: three claims after the glorification

Having established that creation glorifies Him, the ayah states three things about Allah in quick succession.

**"His is the dominion" (lahu al-mulk).** Ibn Kathir explains this together with the next phrase: He is **the One Who has control over all creation.** Ownership here is not a title; it is actual, exercised control over everything that exists.

**"And to Him belongs the praise" (lahu al-ḥamd).** Ibn Kathir glosses this as: He is **the One praised for all He created and decreed.** That word *decreed* is worth pausing on. Praise is due not only for what is obviously pleasant in creation, but for what He has determined.

**"And He is Able to do all things."** Ibn Kathir gives this a precise meaning: **whatever He wills occurs without resistance, and whatever He does not will, never occurs.** Two halves, and both matter. Nothing He intends can be blocked; nothing He has not intended can slip into existence.

## Ayah 2: "He created you — then some of you..."

This is the pivot of the passage. Whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies Him — and then the gaze narrows to the one creature among whom you find both a *kāfir* (a disbeliever) and a *muʾmin* (a believer).

**The little particle that carries the argument.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the *fa* in *fa-minkum* ("then some of you"). This particle, it explains, **denotes "one thing happening after another."** The sequence is therefore: first *khalaqakum* — He created you — and only *then* the division into disbelievers and believers. Maʿārif draws the conclusion directly: the phrase *khalaqakum* **indicates that at the inception of creation there were no unbelievers.** Disbelief, on this reading, is not there at the starting point; it is something that comes afterwards.

**The tradition Maʿārif brings.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān supports this with a Prophetic tradition it cites through Qurṭubī: *"Everyone is born a Muslim, but his parents make him a Jew, a Christian…"* The Arabic of the tradition as Maʿārif gives it says that everyone is born *ʿalā al-fiṭrah* — *fiṭrah* being the word rendered here as being "born a Muslim," the original pattern a person arrives on. Maʿārif cites this through Qurṭubī without naming a ḥadīth collection, so it is best received exactly as it is given, with no collection attached to it.

**How the two commentaries in front of us read this ayah.** Here it is worth being honest that our two sources emphasise different sides of the same ayah, and both are speaking within mainstream Sunni belief.

- **Ibn Kathir** reads it from the side of Allah's will and knowledge: **"Allah created you with these characteristics and He willed that for you. Therefore, there will be believers and disbelievers."** He continues: **"Surely, Allah is the One Who sees those who deserve guidance and those who deserve misguidance."**
- **Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** reads it from the side of human responsibility: human beings **"were, subsequently, divided into believers and non-believers by their own free will and choice with which Allah has invested them. They are rewarded or punished on account of exercising the free will and choice."**

Note the phrasing Maʿārif uses: the free will is itself something **with which Allah has invested them**. Each commentary is given here as it stands, in its own words, without pressing either one into the other.

**"And Allah is All-Seer of what you do."** Ibn Kathir ties this closing phrase to what precedes it: **"He is the Witness over His servant's deeds and He will completely recompense them."** The division of humanity into two is not a label handed out and then forgotten. It is witnessed, and recompensed in full.

## The one brotherhood, and the only line that cuts it

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān builds something socially far-reaching out of ayah 2, under the heading "Two Nations Theory," and it deserves to be given properly.

The Qurʼān here **divides mankind into two groups: a believing group and a non-believing one.** This, Maʿārif says, indicates that the children of Ādam (peace be upon him) are **one single brotherhood**, and all human beings are members of it. *Kufr* — unbelief — is **the only dividing line** that severs relationship with this brotherhood and creates another group. Thus, Maʿārif concludes, group-formation can only take place on the basis of *īmān* and *kufr*.

And then the sharp edge of the point: **neither colour nor language, neither lineage nor family, neither land, territory nor geographical region** can divide human brotherhood into rival groups. Maʿārif offers a plain illustration — the offspring of one father may live in different cities, use different languages, or have different colours, and no sane person would ever regard them as different groups.

Maʿārif then places this against history. **In the Days of Ignorance, ethnicity and tribal divisions had become the basis of factionalism, but the Messenger of Allah ﷺ broke down these idols.** It cites the Qurʼān's own express text — *"All believers are but brothers"* — as establishing that they belong to one brotherhood irrespective of country or territory, colour or family, or language; and it adds that the non-believers likewise, in the sight of Islam, belong to a single community.

There is also a further argument here that is easy to miss. Maʿārif points out that the division by *īmān* and *kufr* **is a matter of free will and choice**: a person who chooses to leave one group and join the other **can do it very easily** — he may give up his articles of faith, choose another faith, and so join the other group. Whereas the affiliations of **race, lineage, colour, language or territory are not within the power or control of anyone.** As Maʿārif puts it, **no one can change his affiliation with his race, colour or language.**

Maʿārif is careful to add that the variety among people is itself evidence of **the perfect power of Allah**, carries many socio-economic benefits, and is **a great blessing** — but that it is **not permitted to use it as the basis of factionalism or group-formation** among mankind. Diversity: a blessing. Diversity as a banner of division: not permitted.

Maʿārif closes this section with grief over the present: Muslims of east and west who were **one nation and one heart**, white and black, Arab and non-Arab, whose might and power the nations of the world could not resist — until the idols shattered by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ were revived once again, the one mighty ummah partitioned into small pieces based on territory, homeland, language, colour, race and lineage, set to collide with one another, clearing the way for the enemies of Islam to attack. This is a commentator's reading of his own times, offered as an application of the ayah rather than as part of its wording — but it shows how much weight one short line of revelation can carry.

## Ayah 3: created with truth, and shaped well

**"He has created the heavens and the earth with truth."** Ibn Kathir explains *bi'l-ḥaqq* as **"with equity and wisdom"** — and the translation given here renders it "for a purpose." Then the ayah moves, within a few words, to "And to Him is the return."

**"And He shaped you and made good your shapes."** Ibn Kathir: **"He made you in the best shapes and forms,"** and he brings two other passages of the Qurʼān alongside it. First, *"O man! What has made you careless about your Lord, the most Generous? Who created you, fashioned you perfectly and gave you due proportion; in whatever form He willed, He put you together"* (82:6–8) — where the same fashioning stands right beside a reproach for carelessness towards the Lord who did it. Second, *"Allah, it is He Who has made for you the earth as a dwelling place and the sky as a canopy, and has given you shape and made your shapes good, and has provided you with good things"* (40:64) — where your form is listed among His favours, between the earth under you and the sky above you.

**Al-Muṣawwir — the Shaper.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens this word up. Shaping the figures of creatures is **one of the exclusive attributes of Allah**, which is why *al-Muṣawwir*, "the shaper," is one of His attributive names. Then it invites you to actually look: the universe holds several classes of things, each class with several species, each species with sexes, each with billions of members — and **no single shape ever resembles another shape.**

Maʿārif presses the point where it is most astonishing, on the human face: a surface of **no more than six to seven square inches**, with uncountable faces of the same type, and yet one face does not look exactly like another so that telling them apart would be difficult. The uniqueness of each individual's face and shape, Maʿārif says, is so amazing that **it baffles the human imagination.**

And then the phrase that follows in the ayah — *"and made your figures good."* Maʿārif notes that the verse mentions figure-making as one of the Divine blessings and immediately adds this. Its comment is one of the kindest lines in the passage: **in the entire universe, Allah made the human shape the most beautiful**, and no matter how ugly a person might seem in his own community, **he is still beautiful in his own right**, relative to the shapes of all other non-human creatures.

**"And to Him is the return."** Ibn Kathir gives it plainly: **the return and final destination.**

## Ayah 4: knowledge that reaches into the chest

The passage now closes the circle it opened. Ayah 1 said whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies Him; ayah 4 says **He knows what is in the heavens and on earth.**

Then the ayah moves inward in two steps. First, **"He knows what you conceal and what you reveal"** — the hidden and the public are named together. Second, **"And Allah is the All-Knower of what is in the breasts."** Ibn Kathir introduces the ayah by saying that Allah **informs of His knowledge of all that there is in the heavens, in the earth and in the souls.**

That is the arc Ibn Kathir traces: the heavens, the earth, and the souls. Ayah 2 had already said He is **All-Seer of what you do**; ayah 4 adds that He is All-Knower of what is in the breasts. Outward act and inward state alike lie open to Him.

## Living it

Read as one unit, these four ayat ask a few concrete things:

**Join what is already happening.** All creatures praise the glory of Allah, their Creator and Owner. The believer's *tasbīḥ* — declaring Allah's glory — is not an odd act of piety inserted into a neutral universe; it is falling into step with it.

**Praise Him for the decree, not only for the gift.** Ibn Kathir's gloss on *lahu al-ḥamd* — praised for all He **created and decreed** — takes praise beyond the moments when life is pleasant.

**Let ayah 1 settle your fear.** If whatever He wills occurs without resistance, and whatever He does not will never occurs, then nothing that reaches you arrived outside His will, and nothing withheld from you was taken out of His hand.

**Guard the only division that counts.** Maʿārif's reading of ayah 2 is not abstract. Loyalty organised around colour, language, tribe, or territory is exactly the factionalism it says the Messenger of Allah ﷺ broke down — while the variety among people itself remains, in Maʿārif's words, a great blessing.

**Do not despise your own form, or anyone else's.** You were shaped by al-Muṣawwir, uniquely, and — as Maʿārif insists — beautifully in your own right.

**Do not treat the inward as unseen.** The passage ends with what is in the breasts. Ibn Kathir's summary of it — the heavens, the earth, and the souls — leaves nothing outside His knowledge.

passages.title: The fate of earlier deniers of messengers
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** The sūrah turns from the individual to history: whole nations before us heard the call of Allah's Messengers, opposed them, denied the truth, and were ruined. Ayah 5 shows the outcome — they *tasted* the evil result of what they did. Ayah 6 then gives the reason: their Messengers came to them with clear proofs, and they threw the message away over a single objection — that the messenger was a human being like themselves. The two ayat form one movement, effect first and reason after, so that the listener meets the punishment before he is told how it was earned.

Ibn Kathir titles this passage exactly that way: *A Warning delivered through mentioning the End of the Disbelieving Nations*. Allah, he says, is informing us about the past nations and the torment and disciplinary lessons that they suffered because of opposing the Messengers and denying the truth.

## "Has the news of those who disbelieved before not reached you?"

The ayah opens as a question, but Ibn Kathir's heading tells us what kind of question it is: a **warning**, not an enquiry. It is not gathering information from the listener; it is placing him in front of something he is assumed to have heard already, and leaving him to answer for what he does with it.

The word rendered "news" is **naba'**. Ibn Kathir glosses it simply: *information about them and what happened to them*. Notice where the weight falls — not on who those nations were, but on **what happened to them**. History here is not offered as curiosity. It is offered as evidence.

**"So they tasted the evil result of their affair."** The Arabic is `فَذَاقُوا وَبَالَ أَمْرِهِمْ`, and Ibn Kathir explains it: *they tasted the evil consequences of their denial and sinful actions.*

Two things are worth sitting with.

*Dhāqū* — **they tasted**. Tasting is the most intimate way of encountering a thing. You can hear about something, or see it at a distance, and remain outside it; tasting admits no such distance. The image the ayah chooses closes the gap between the warning and the ones warned. What had been words became something in their own mouths.

*Wabāl* — the **evil outcome, the bitter consequence**. And Ibn Kathir attaches it precisely: to **their** denial and **their** sinful actions. Nothing foreign was imposed on them. What they swallowed was the consequence of their own conduct.

**"And for them is a painful punishment."** Here the ayah steps from one world into the next, and Ibn Kathir is precise about the seam. The tasting, he says, refers to the punishment and humiliation they received **in the life of this world**. The painful torment is **in the Hereafter, added to the torment they received in this life**.

That word **added** is the whole point. A reader could easily assume that a nation destroyed in this world has thereby paid its bill — that the ruin settled the account. Ibn Kathir says otherwise. The worldly punishment was the first taste, not the total.

Note also the two things he names for this world: punishment **and humiliation**. The loss was not only in what happened to them but in how they were left.

## The reason, and how small it was

**"That was because their messengers used to come to them with clear proofs."** *Dhālika bi-annahu* — *that was because* — is the hinge of the passage. Ibn Kathir marks it plainly: **Allah explained why**. Everything in ayah 5 is now given its cause. The proof came before the punishment.

They came **bil-bayyināt**. Ibn Kathir unpacks the word as **supporting arguments, evidence, and clear proofs**. This matters, because the ayah is about to show us people rejecting a message that had arrived with exactly that. Their problem was never a shortage of clarity.

**"But they said: Shall mere mortals guide us?"** — `أَبَشَرٌ يَهْدُونَنَا`. This is the entire objection. Not "your proofs are weak." Not "your teaching is false." Simply: *a human being? Guiding us?*

Ibn Kathir reads their posture exactly: **they discounted and dismissed the possibility** that the Message would be sent to a human, and that their guidance would come by the hands of a man like themselves. It is the language of dismissal, not of examination. Set that beside what they had just been given — supporting arguments, evidence, clear proofs — and the imbalance is the lesson. Everything necessary for belief had reached them; what they returned was a remark about the messenger.

**A grammatical detail worth pausing on.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that although the word **bashar** ("mortal," "human being") is singular in form, it is **plural in meaning** here — which is why the verb attached to it, *yahdūnanā* ("they guide us"), comes in the plural. So the sneer is not aimed at one individual only. The Arabic itself widens the complaint from a single prophet to the line of prophets — which is precisely what the ayah is documenting, since it speaks of *their Messengers* coming to *them*, people after people.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the general rule out plainly: **all the unbelievers held the notion that prophets and messengers cannot be human beings**, and the Qur'an has time and again falsified and refuted this notion.

**"So they disbelieved and turned away."** Ibn Kathir separates the two verbs, and the separation is instructive: *they denied the truth* — that is *kafarū* — *and turned away from abiding by it* — that is *tawallaw*. A rejection held inwardly, and then a life ordered around that rejection. The denial did not stay a denial; it became a refusal to live by what they had been shown.

## "But Allah was not in need"

`وَاسْتَغْنَى اللَّهُ` — Ibn Kathir gives the shortest possible gloss, and it is enough: **Allah had no need — of them.**

Whatever those nations imagined they were withholding, the ayah answers in three words. Their refusal took nothing from Allah. The consequences of it, as ayah 5 has already shown, fell entirely on them.

Then the ayah closes on two of the beautiful names: **`وَاللَّهُ غَنِيٌّ حَمِيدٌ`** — *and Allah is Free of all need, Worthy of all praise.*

**Al-Ghaniyy.** Free of all need — so the historical statement ("Allah had no need of them") rests on something permanent, not on a particular moment of history. What happened with those nations was not an exception in how Allah deals with creation.

**Al-Hamīd.** Worthy of all praise — praise is His due, whether or not it is offered.

The two names sit together in one phrase. He is utterly free of need from His creation, and utterly deserving of all praise. As with all the divine attributes, we affirm these as Allah affirmed them for Himself, without likening them to anything in creation and without emptying them of their meaning.

## A caution for the believers

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān turns this passage back on the Muslim reader in a way that is easy to miss. The unbelievers erred by refusing to accept that a mortal could carry the message. But there is also, Maʿārif notes, **a group of Muslims who deny the mortality of Allah's Messenger ﷺ** — his being *bashar*, a human being — and, it says frankly, they need to think about which direction they are moving in.

The correction it offers is careful and worth holding exactly as stated:

- His mortality is **not contradictory to his prophethood**.
- It is **not incompatible with his high station of messengership**.
- And his being a Messenger is **not inconsistent with his being Nūr (light)**.

He is Nūr **and** he is a mortal; the two are not rivals. Maʿārif adds one further guard: it is a **false analogy** to compare his light with that of a lamp, or of the sun, or of the moon.

In other words, the answer to one error is not the opposite error. The deniers of ayah 6 could not accept that a mortal carried the message; some later admirers cannot accept that the one carrying it was a mortal. The Qur'an, as Maʿārif says, has refuted that notion again and again.

## Living it

**Take the news as evidence, not as entertainment.** Ibn Kathir calls this passage a warning delivered through mentioning the end of the disbelieving nations, and the ayah assumes the news has already reached you. What is being tested is not your knowledge of what happened to earlier peoples but whether that knowledge changes anything in you.

**Watch what the objection was actually aimed at.** They did not dispute the supporting arguments, the evidence, or the clear proofs. They disputed the messenger — *shall mere mortals guide us?* When we find ourselves resisting a truth by discussing the person who brought it rather than the proof he brought, the ayah has already named the manoeuvre.

**Do not answer one error with its opposite.** Maʿārif's caution stands over both ditches: refusing a human messenger, and refusing to let the messenger ﷺ be human. Neither is loyalty to what Allah actually did.

**And know who is served by your obedience.** *Allah was not in need* — of them, or of anyone. He is Ghaniyy, Hamīd: free of all need, worthy of all praise whether we join in or not. The invitation still standing in front of us is not a favour we do Him.

passages.title: Resurrection denied, and the Day of Mutual Loss
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat take the denial that stands behind so much rejection of the message — "there is no resurrection" — and answer it with an oath, a command, and a scene. Ayah 7 reports the denial and swears it down; ayah 8 turns the reader from argument to action ("so believe"); ayah 9 opens the curtain on the Day itself and names it *at-Taghābun*, the Day of Loss and Gain; ayah 10 closes the two files that the naming implies. What holds the passage together is that name: everything before it establishes that the Day is coming, and everything after it shows what is won and lost when it arrives.

## "They claim they will not be raised" (ayah 7)

Ibn Kathir opens simply: Allah is informing us about "the disbelievers, idolators and the atheists" — that they claim they will not be resurrected. Note that the denial is reported as a *claim* (the translation before you renders it "claim"; Ibn Kathir's rendering has "pretend"). It is an assertion put forward, not a case proved. And the Qur'an does not meet it here with a long argument. It meets it with something heavier.

**The oath.** The reply begins بَلَىٰ — rendered "Yes!" Then comes the oath: **وَرَبِّي** — "By my Lord, you will certainly be resurrected." Ibn Kathir notes that this is the third ayah in which Allah orders His Messenger ﷺ to swear by his Lord, the Exalted and Most Honored, that the Resurrection occurs, and he names the other two:

- **Sūrah Yūnus 10:53** — "And they ask you to inform them: 'Is it true?' Say: 'Yes! By my Lord! It is the very truth! and you can not escape it!'"
- **Sūrah Sabaʼ 34:3** — "Those who disbelieve say: 'The Hour will not come to us.' Say: 'Yes, by my Lord, it will come to you.'"
- **This ayah, 64:7.**

In each of the three, a denial of the Hereafter is put forward, and in each the Prophet ﷺ is commanded to answer it with an oath by his Lord.

**"Then you will surely be informed of what you did."** Ibn Kathir explains the meaning: "you will be informed of all of your actions, whether major or minor, big or small." Resurrection, as this ayah presents it, is not bare re-existence. It is followed immediately by disclosure. To be raised is to be shown your own life, complete, with nothing filed away out of sight.

**"And that is easy for Allah."** Ibn Kathir: "resurrecting and recompensing you is easy for Allah." Both halves — the raising and the reckoning — are easy for Him. The denier's difficulty was never with the evidence; it was that he measured the act against his own imagination of what is possible. The ayah quietly removes the measuring stick.

## "So believe in Allah, and His Messenger, and the Light We have sent down" (ayah 8)

The "so, therefore" at the head of ayah 8 makes this the conclusion drawn from the oath. If the Day is certain and your deeds will be read back to you, then the move the ayah calls for is to believe now.

Three objects of faith are named. **The Light**, both Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explain, is the Qur'an. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out why the word is so exact: light fulfils two functions — it is itself luminous, and it makes other things luminous and bright. The Qur'an, on account of its miraculous nature, is itself luminous; and it illuminates what pleases and displeases Allah, the sacred laws, injunctions and commands, and the realities of the Hereafter which a human being ought to know. That last item is precisely what this passage is doing. The reader who cannot see the Day of Gathering by his own eyesight is being handed the lamp by which it becomes visible.

**"And Allah is All-Aware of what you do."** The word is *Khabīr*, All-Aware. Ibn Kathir's gloss is one line: "none of your deeds ever escapes His knowledge." Placed here, it seals the argument — the file that will be read out on that Day is being compiled now, by One from whom nothing slips.

## The Day of Gathering (ayah 9)

"The Day when He will gather you on the Day of Gathering" — Ibn Kathir: this means the Day of Resurrection. Picture it as he describes it: the earlier and later generations all gathered in one area, a caller who would be heard by them all, and one's vision able to see them all. He cites two other ayat for the same scene: "That is the Day whereon mankind will be gathered together, that is a Day when all will be present" (11:103), and "Say: '(Yes) verily, those of old, and those of later times. All will surely be gathered together for appointed meeting of a known Day'" (56:49–50).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the reason for the name: on that day all creations, the earlier generations as well as the later, will be brought together to give account of their deeds and for reward and punishment. The gathering is not the point; the accounting is.

## *At-Taghābun*: the Day of Loss and Gain

Here the sūrah gets its name, and here is where the passage rewards slow reading.

**The root.** *Taghābun* is derived from **ghabn**, which means loss. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that both financial loss and mental deficiency are referred to as *ghabn*. It cites Imām Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī's *Mufradāt al-Qurʼān*: when the word refers to financial loss it is expressed in the passive voice — *ghubina fulānun*, "so-and-so suffered financial loss"; but to say that someone became deficient in his opinion or judgement, the form is *ghabina*, the middle letter vowelled with a kasrah, on the measure of *samiʿa*.

**The pattern.** *Taghābun*, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, is a two-way process signifying mutuality of actions, where two parties mutually cause each other loss, or make manifest each other's loss. In the context of this ayah, however, it is a one-way process: the making manifest of the non-believer's loss — and that sense too is a recognised use of the form.

**The classical explanations.** Ibn ʿAbbās said: "It is one of the names of the Day of Judgement, and that is because the people of Paradise will have gained over the people of the Fire." Qatādah and Mujāhid said similarly. Muqātil bin Ḥayyān put it most starkly: "There is no mutual loss and gain greater than these entering Paradise and those being taken to the Fire."

**The two abodes.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that, according to authentic Traditions — elaborately recorded, it says, in the two Ṣaḥīḥs and other collections — Allah has created two abodes for everyone in the Hereafter: one in Hell and one in Paradise. Before the righteous believers are admitted to Paradise they will be shown the abode in Hell which they would have received had they failed to believe and act righteously, so that they may appreciate their abode in Paradise more highly and thank Allah more profoundly. The non-believers will be shown their abode in Paradise, which they would have received had they believed and acted righteously, so that they may regret more bitterly. And the exchange is completed: the abodes in Paradise prepared for the non-believers will be given to the believers, and the abodes in Hell prepared for the believers will be given to the non-believers. When the inmates of Paradise attain the places originally prepared for the disbelievers, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, the latter will realise what they have lost and what the others have gained. That is the moment the name of this sūrah describes.

## The loss that reaches the believer too

Ibn ʿAbbās and the other leading authorities on tafsīr gave the explanation above. But Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that other authorities express a further view, and it is the one that should keep a believer awake. On that Day the grief of loss will be felt not only by the non-believers. The righteous believers will feel it too — bitterly regretting that they wasted much of their time in life and failed to carry out more good deeds, deeds that would have won them more blessings and favours in Paradise.

The commentary cites a saying of the Prophet ﷺ to this effect: he who sits in an assembly and does not remember Allah in the entire session — that assembly will be a source of bitter regret for him on the Day of Resurrection. (The source here does not name a collection, so it is passed on as a teaching without attribution to a specific book.)

Qurṭubī writes that on that Day every believer will feel a sense of loss on account of shortcomings in the fulfilment of his duties and obligations in life. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then observes that naming the Day of Judgement "the Day of Loss and Gain" is like its being named "the Day of (Bitter) Regret" in Sūrah Maryam: "And warn them of the Day of (Bitter) Regret when the affair will be resolved" (19:39). *Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī* reads that ayah as implying that on that Day the unjust and unrighteous will bitterly regret their shortcomings, and the righteous believers will regret their shortcomings in the performance of their righteous deeds — so that everyone on that Day will have some feeling of regret and loss over what he fell short in. Hence, it concludes, the name.

## From the Sunnah: how a full account goes empty

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān brings two hadith at this point that show *ghabn* happening to someone who thought he was in profit.

**The pauper.** Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, Tirmidhī and others record, on the authority of Sayyidnā Abū Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked the noble Companions: "Do you know who is a pauper?" They replied: "One who has no possessions." He ﷺ said that the pauper of his community is one who will come on the Day of Judgement with a heap of righteous deeds — prayers, fasting, alms-giving and so on — but who had reviled someone in the world, or slandered another, or killed someone, or taken someone's property unlawfully. All these people gather round him and demand their rights: one takes away his prayers, another snatches his fasts, another carries off his alms and his other good deeds. When all his good deeds are exhausted, the sins of the oppressed are loaded onto the oppressor, and in this way the score is settled — and so he is pushed into the Fire.

**The debt to be settled here.** It is recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥ of Bukhārī that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever has an obligation towards someone should discharge it or ask his obligor to forgive it here in this world. Otherwise, he will have no dirhams or dinars (money) there in the Hereafter to set off his liabilities. The obligors will be given the good deeds of the debtor in lieu of their unfulfilled rights. When his good deeds will be exhausted, the sins of the oppressed will be added to the account of the oppressor."

Put these beside the name *at-Taghābun* and it becomes concrete. The man in the first hadith was not short of worship. He was short of *net* worship — undone by his own tongue and his own hands.

## The two files closed (ayat 9–10)

Having named the Day, Allah explains His statement, as Ibn Kathir puts it, by setting out the two outcomes.

**"And whosoever believes in Allah and performs righteous deeds, He will expiate from him his sins, and will admit him to Gardens beneath which rivers flow, to dwell therein forever; that will be the great success."** Note the order: faith, then righteous action, then the expiation of evil deeds, then admission, then permanence. Sin is not overlooked; it is *expiated* — cancelled by the One with the authority to cancel it. And the word for success is *al-fawz al-ʿaẓīm*, the great success — the Qur'an's own verdict on the winning side of the exchange.

**"But those who disbelieved and denied Our Ayat, they will be the dwellers of the Fire, to dwell therein forever. And worst indeed is that destination."** The two conditions named for this side are the two the passage opened with: disbelief, and the denial of Allah's *āyāt*, His signs and verses. This is the same denial reported in ayah 7 and the same Light offered in ayah 8, now shown at its end point.

## Living it

The passage moves from an argument to a choice, so it asks something concrete:

**Take the oath seriously.** Ibn Kathir counts three places where the Prophet ﷺ is commanded to swear by his Lord that the Resurrection occurs. It is not presented as an open question. Let the certainty of it press on ordinary decisions — that is what belief in it is *for*.

**Assume disclosure.** "You will be informed of what you did" — and Ibn Kathir specifies: major or minor, big or small. Nothing is beneath the record.

**Settle your accounts now.** Both hadith point at the same door, and it is open only in this life. Return what was taken. Ask forgiveness of the person you wronged. In the Hereafter, as the hadith says, there are no dirhams or dinars with which to settle — only deeds.

**Fill the empty hours.** If a believer's own regret on that Day will be over time wasted and good deeds not done, then the cure begins today, in the ordinary gatherings and idle stretches that a person assumes cost him nothing.

**And be grateful in advance.** The narrations describe believers being shown the abode they escaped precisely so that they may value what they were given and thank Allah more profoundly. A believer who occasionally lets himself see the alternative — and thanks Allah for guidance he did not manufacture himself — is already practising, in this world, the response he will have on that Day.

passages.title: Affliction by Allah's will and trusting Him
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat move through three things in order: where hardship comes from, what we are commanded to do, and whom we are to rely on. Ayah 11 places every calamity under Allah's permission and promises the believing heart guidance in return; ayah 12 commands obedience to Allah and to His Messenger ﷺ; ayah 13 names the One in whom all of this is anchored — there is no god except Him — and directs believers to place their trust in Him.

## "No calamity befalls anyone except by Allah's Will" (ayah 11)

The opening statement is absolute. Ibn Kathir connects it to what Allah says in Sūrat al-Ḥadīd: *"No calamity occurs on the earth or in yourselves but it is inscribed in a record before We bring it into existence. Verily, that is easy for Allah"* (57:22). Read together, the two verses give two facts about any hardship: it was written down before it came into existence, and it arrives only by Allah's permission.

**"By the permission of Allah."** Ibn 'Abbas glossed this phrase more strongly still: *"By the command of Allah,"* which Ibn Kathir explains as meaning **from His decree and will**. So this is not a passive "Allah allowed it to slip through." It is His decree and His will — nothing reaches you around Him.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the principle in its widest form: **not even a particle can move without the Divine will, and without the will of Allah no one can harm or benefit anyone.** That last clause is worth sitting with, because it is precisely what a frightened heart forgets. The person who wronged you, the illness, the loss, the one who withheld what you needed — none of them possess independent power to harm or to benefit.

**Note what the ayah does not say.** It does not say the calamity is painless, or that you must pretend it did not hurt. It says where it came from.

## "And whoever believes in Allah, He guides his heart"

The second half of ayah 11 is the promise, and it is phrased as a condition: *whoever* believes, *He guides his heart*.

Ibn Kathir unpacks who exactly is meant: **whoever suffered an affliction and knew that it occurred by Allah's judgement and decree, and patiently abides, awaiting Allah's reward** — that person Allah guides in his heart. Notice the three things stacked together in his description: knowledge (that this is from Allah's judgement and decree), patience (he abides), and expectation of reward (he is awaiting what Allah has promised). Belief here is not an abstract creed; it is what a person does with his heart at the moment the blow lands.

And what is the payment? Ibn Kathir says Allah **compensates him for his loss in this life by granting guidance to his heart and certainty in faith**, and that **Allah will replace whatever he lost for Him with the same or what is better.** Read that carefully: the first compensation named is not a replacement of the thing lost — it is the heart itself being put right. You lose something outward and are given something inward.

**What certainty sounds like.** 'Ali bin Abi Talhah reported from Ibn 'Abbas on this phrase: *"Allah will guide his heart to certainty. Therefore, he will know that what reached him would not have missed him and what has missed him would not have reached him."*

Sit with that sentence, because it speaks to two torments at once. What struck you was never going to miss you — so the endless replaying of what you should have done differently is chasing a thing that was never available. And what missed you was never going to reach you — so the door you did not get through was not, in Allah's decree, your door. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān repeats the same formula: the believer is guided to the certainty that **whatever difficulty afflicts him could never have missed him, and whatever adversity has missed him could never have afflicted him.**

**"And Allah is the All-Knower of everything."** The ayah seals itself with this. The One who decreed the affliction is not distant from it or unaware of what it cost. His knowledge encompasses everything.

## Two ways to receive a blow

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the contrast that makes this passage land practically. **The person who does not believe in Allah and in the Divine destination has no means of comforting himself when a calamity befalls him.** He receives it with despair, and gropes for means of alleviating it.

The believer, on the other hand, who reposes his faith in Divine will and destination is guided by Allah, and **his heart is filled with peace and tranquility.** The circumstances have not changed — the loss is still a loss. What has changed is that he knows Whose decree it came by, and, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, he is promised a reward in the Hereafter which he keeps in view all the time. Its conclusion is striking: **this strong belief in the promise of a reward in the Hereafter alleviates the worst calamity of this world.** Not merely the small trials — the worst of them.

## From the Sunnah

Ibn Kathir cites here an agreed-upon hadith, which Al-Bukhari and Muslim collected, in which it is stated:

> *Amazing is the believer: There is no decree that Allah writes for him, but is better for him. If an affliction strikes him, he is patient and this is better for him. If a bounty is granted to him, he is thankful and this is better for him. This trait is only for the faithful believer.*

Look at what the hadith adds to the ayah. The ayah tells you where hardship comes from; the hadith tells you that **every** decree Allah writes for a believer is better for him — hardship and ease alike. And it names what stands in each case: patience under affliction, thankfulness under bounty. The hadith closes by saying this trait belongs to no one but the faithful believer. Life hands everyone the same two categories of event; the hadith ties the good outcome of both to faith.

## "Obey Allah and obey the Messenger" (ayah 12)

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah here **commands obedience to Him and to His Messenger ﷺ in all that He legislates and in implementing His orders**, and that **Allah also forbids one from all that His Messenger ﷺ forbids and prohibits.** So obedience has two halves — doing what is commanded and abstaining from what is prohibited — and the Messenger's ﷺ prohibitions are named alongside Allah's commands.

**"But if you turn away…"** The consequence stated is unexpected. It does not threaten punishment at this point; it states the limit of the Messenger's ﷺ charge: *then the duty of Our Messenger is only to convey clearly.* Ibn Kathir explains the meaning: if you refrain from abiding by the faith, then the Messenger's mission is to convey, and your mission is to hear and obey.

Az-Zuhri summed up the division of labour in a line Ibn Kathir preserves: *"From Allah comes the Message, its deliverance is up to the Messenger, and the adherence is up to us."* Three parties, three tasks — and the third is the one named as ours.

## "Allah — there is no god except Him" (ayah 13)

The passage ends by naming its foundation. Ibn Kathir explains that Allah here **states that He is the One whom all creations need and seek, the One other than whom there is no true god.**

That phrase — *whom all creations need and seek* — carries the weight of the ayah. Everything else is among the creations that stand in need; He alone is the One they need.

**Tawḥīd, then reliance.** Ibn Kathir observes the order: **He first informs about Tawḥīd and its meaning**, and the implied meaning is **to single Him out for deification, being purely devoted to Him, and relying upon Him.** On Ibn Kathir's reading, then, reliance is not something separate from the declaration; it is part of what "there is no god except Him" implies. He supports this with Allah's words: *"The Lord of the east and the west; La ilaha illa Huwa. So take Him alone as Trustee"* (73:9) — where the same movement occurs: first the declaration, then "take Him alone as Trustee."

**"So let the believers put their trust in Allah."** Note who is addressed — **the believers**. Trust in Allah is set out here as what belief calls for, not as an optional temperament.

## Living it

Put the three ayat together and you have a shape for meeting hardship:

**Trace it back.** Whatever has struck you occurred by Allah's decree and will — not by the unchecked power of any person or circumstance. It was inscribed in a record before it came into existence.

**Hold on and expect the reward.** Ibn Kathir's believer is one who knows it came by Allah's judgement and decree, patiently abides, and is *awaiting Allah's reward*.

**Let the "if only" go.** What reached you would not have missed you; what missed you would not have reached you. That is the certainty Ibn 'Abbas says Allah guides the believer's heart to.

**Obey.** The Messenger's ﷺ mission was to convey clearly, and he has conveyed; the adherence, as Az-Zuhri said, is up to us.

**Entrust.** Say and mean *lā ilāha illā Huwa*, and let your reliance rest where the declaration points — "and in Allah therefore let the believers put their trust."

The promise embedded in ayah 11 is quietly enormous. Ibn Kathir says Allah will replace whatever was lost for His sake with the same or with something better — but the compensation he names first is guidance of the heart and certainty in faith. That is what this ayah promises the one who receives the blow as a believer.

passages.title: Family and wealth as tests; spending well
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat bring Surah At-Taghabun to its close — and they bring it home, into the house. The surah's final word is not about open warfare against faith; it is about the pull of the people and the property you love most. The unit holds together as a single movement: a warning (ayah 14), a diagnosis (ayah 15), a prescription (ayah 16), an astonishing offer (ayah 17), and a closing seal of divine names that guarantees the whole transaction (ayah 18).

## The situation these words came into

The strongest key to ayah 14 is the moment it was revealed. Ibn Kathir records, through Ibn Abi Hatim, that Ibn 'Abbas was asked about this ayah by a man, and explained: there were men who embraced Islam in Makkah and wanted to migrate to Allah's Messenger ﷺ — but their wives and children refused to let them go. Later, when they finally did join him ﷺ, they found that the Companions who were already with him had gained knowledge in the religion. Seeing what they had missed, they were about to punish their wives and children for having held them back. It was then that Allah sent down the second half of the ayah: **"But if you pardon and overlook, and forgive, then verily, Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful."** At-Tirmidhi collected this hadith and said that it is *Hasan Sahih*.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same account (from Tirmidhi, Hakim and others, with an authentic chain of transmitters, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas), adding the detail that makes the emotional stakes clear: this was the time when it was compulsory for every Muslim to migrate from Makkah. So the family was not merely being difficult. They were standing in the way of loyalty and obedience to a divine law — and, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, none can be a greater enemy than one who involves a person in eternal punishment.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also carries a second occasion, reported by 'Ata' Ibn Rabah: the ayah was revealed in connection with 'Awf Ibn Malik al-Ashja'i. Whenever the occasion to go out for jihad arose and he intended to participate, his wife and children would complain, *"In whose care are you leaving us?"* — and he would be influenced by their complaint and change his mind. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the two narratives do not conflict; each in its own right can be the cause of revelation, because — in its words — a wife and children who stand in the way of obeying Allah's laws, whether migration or jihad, become the enemies of Allah.

## "Some of" — the exactness of ayah 14

Read the wording carefully. It is not *your spouses and your children are enemies to you*. It is: **"Indeed, some of your spouses and children are enemies."** The Arabic *min* ("among / some of") narrows the statement to a portion, not the whole. The Qur'an is not slandering family; it is warning that within the circle of those you love, some may function as an enemy — and the ayah does not even say they intend it.

That is the force of the word **'aduww (enemy)**. Ibn Kathir explains the sense: some wives and children are enemies to their husbands and fathers "in that they might be busied with them rather than with performing the good deeds." Mujahid explained the ayah by saying: "They might direct the man to sever his relation or disobey his Lord. The man, who loves his wives and children, might obey them in this case." The enmity, in other words, is usually not hostility. It is *leverage* — the leverage that love itself gives them over you. Ibn Kathir draws the parallel to the ayah in the previous surah: *"O you who believe! Let not your properties or your children divert you from the remembrance of Allah. And whosoever does that, then they are the losers"* (63:9).

**"Therefore beware of them!"** — and Ibn Zayd supplies the crucial qualifier: beware of them *for your religion*. The guard being posted is around your obedience to Allah.

## The turn nobody expects

Then ayah 14 does something remarkable. Having just called some of them enemies, it does not authorise a single reprisal. Instead it stacks three verbs of release — **pardon, overlook, forgive** — and answers them with two of Allah's own names: *Ghafur, Rahim*, the Oft-Forgiving, the Most Merciful. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the sequence exactly as the story requires: the Muslims who had been warned by the previous part of the verse that their wives and children were their enemies decided they would treat their family members harshly, and this part of the verse was revealed on that occasion — to say that although they had indeed behaved like enemies and stood in the way of your duty towards Allah, you are not to treat them harshly and mercilessly, but rather politely and leniently. This is better for you, because Allah loves forgiving and showing mercy.

**A ruling drawn from this.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that scholars have deduced from this verse that if family members do anything in violation of the sacred laws, it is not appropriate to be disappointed with them totally, or to be hostile towards them, or to hate or curse them.

That single sentence rescues the ayah from every misuse. The warning is for your own vigilance; it is not a licence to punish the people in your house.

## Ayah 15: what a *fitnah* actually is

Ayah 15 widens the lens from spouses and children to **wealth and children**, and renames the whole thing: *"Your wealth and your children are only a fitnah."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the plain meaning of the word: *fitnah* means **test or trial**. And it spells out what the test measures — whether a man becomes so engrossed in the love of wealth and children that he grows heedless of Allah's laws and injunctions, or whether he maintains that love within limits and remains mindful of his duties towards Allah.

Ibn Kathir puts it the same way: wealth and children are a test and trial from Allah for His creatures, so that He knows those who obey Him and those who disobey Him.

Notice what the ayah does *not* say. It does not say wealth and children are evil, or a punishment, or something to escape. It says they are the exam paper. The same child can be the reason a man works honestly and the reason he cuts corners; the same wealth can be the reason he gives and the reason he hoards.

And the ayah does not leave you with the warning alone: *"whereas Allah! With Him is a great reward."* Ibn Kathir explains "with Him" as meaning **on the Day of Resurrection** — the reward is real but deferred, which is precisely why the near, touchable reward of family and property is so hard to weigh against it. He connects it to the great ayah on the same theme: *"Beautified for men is the love of things they covet — women, children, heaped-up treasures of gold and silver, branded beautiful horses, cattle and well-tilled land. This is the pleasure of the present world's life; but Allah has the excellent return with Him"* (3:14).

## The Prophet ﷺ shows what he means

The most beautiful commentary on ayah 15 is an action, not a sentence. Imam Ahmad recorded that Buraydah said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was giving a speech when al-Hasan and Husayn came in wearing red shirts, walking and tripping. He ﷺ descended from the minbar, held them, placed them in front of him, and said:

> "Allah and His Messenger said the truth — *'Verily, your wealth and your children are a fitnah.'* I saw these two boys walking and tripping and could not be patient until I stopped my speech and picked them up."

This was recorded by the Sunan compilers, and At-Tirmidhi said: *"Hasan Gharib."*

He ﷺ did not say this to condemn himself. He said it to *define the word*. A fitnah is exactly this: the thing so dear that it pulls you mid-sentence. He named the pull honestly, in public, from the minbar — and then he picked up the children anyway. The ayah is not asking you to stop loving them. It is asking you to know what that love can do to you, and to keep your eyes open while you feel it.

## The sharper warnings

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān does not soften the danger. The truth of the matter, it says, is that the love of wealth and children is a great trial for man; he mostly commits sins for their love, especially when he indulges in earning a livelihood through unlawful means. It relates that according to a hadith, some people will be brought on the Day of Judgment and the people will look at such a man and say, *"His family ate up his good deeds."* And it relates that in another narration the Prophet ﷺ, referring to children, said they are **مَبْخَلَة مَجْبَنَة** — *a cause of one's miserliness and cowardice*: on account of their love a man fails to spend in Allah's way, and on account of their love he fails to participate in jihad. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives both of these without naming a collection, so they are conveyed here as it gives them.)

Some righteous elders have said: *al-'iyal susu'l-ta'at* — **"Family is the weevil of obedience."** A weevil is a small beetle that feeds on grain and seeds and destroys crops; likewise, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, a family feeds on a man's good deeds and destroys them. Nothing looks wrong from outside the sack. That is the image: your acts of obedience can be hollowed out from within by the very people you are obeying Allah for.

## Ayah 16: four commands, and the mercy in the first

Ayah 16 answers the diagnosis with a prescription of four imperatives: **have taqwa of Allah as much as you can, listen, obey, and spend.**

*Taqwa* is mindfulness of Allah — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān glosses it as total obedience to Allah in awe of Him. And the qualifier attached to it here, *ma istata'tum* ("as much as you can"), is one of the great mercies in the Qur'an. Ibn Kathir explains it as: as much as you are able and can bear or endure.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the background that shows why this mattered so much. When the verse *"Observe taqwa of Allah as is His due"* (3:102) was revealed, the blessed Companions felt it very difficult, because it was impossible for anyone to observe taqwa of Allah *as is due to Him*. On that occasion the present verse was revealed, clarifying that no imposition is made on man more than he can bear; taqwa too must be observed as far as it is possible for a person to observe.

This principle is confirmed in the Sunnah. The Two Sahihs recorded that Abu Hurayrah said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "When I command you to do something, do as much as you can of it, and whatever I forbid for you, then avoid it."

Note the asymmetry the hadith preserves: commands are scaled to capacity, prohibitions are to be avoided outright. You are not asked for a perfection you do not have — but you are asked for everything you do have.

**"Listen and obey."** Ibn Kathir explains: obey what Allah and His Messenger ﷺ command you to do, and do not stray from it to the right or left; do not utter a statement or make a decision before Allah and His Messenger ﷺ issue a statement or decision; do not ignore what you were ordered to do, nor commit what you were forbidden from doing.

**"And spend in charity — that is better for yourselves."** Ibn Kathir makes the object concrete: give from what Allah has granted you to your relatives, the poor, the needy and the weak. Be kind to Allah's creatures, just as Allah was and still is kind with you. This will be better for you in this life and the Hereafter — and if you do not do it, it will be worse for you in this life and the Hereafter.

See how tightly this answers the passage's own diagnosis. If wealth and family are the test, then the antidote to being owned by them is to release some of what you hold, deliberately and regularly.

## The one thing standing in the way

*"And whosoever is saved from his own greed — then they are the successful ones."*

The word rendered "greed" is **shuhh** — the tight-fistedness of the soul itself. And the verb is passive: *whoever is **saved** from it*. You do not simply decide your way out of stinginess; you are protected from it. That is why the ayah ends with *al-muflihun*, "the successful ones" — the ones who truly come out ahead. Ibn Kathir notes that he has already explained this with a similar ayah in Surat al-Hashr, where he also mentioned the relevant hadiths, and so does not repeat them here.

## Ayah 17: Allah asks you for a loan

Then comes the offer that ought to stop the reader in place: *"If you lend to Allah a handsome loan, He will double it for you, and will forgive you."*

Ibn Kathir's gloss is simple: whatever you spend, Allah will replace it, and on Him will be the reward of whatever you give away in charity. And he observes that Allah considered giving charity as if it were a **loan to Him** — *qard hasan*, a goodly loan — just as Allah said in a Qudsi Hadith: *"Who will give a loan to He Who is neither unjust nor poor?"* That is, to a Borrower who will never wrong you and will never be unable to repay. Ibn Kathir links this to Surat al-Baqarah: *"...so that He may multiply it to him many times over"* (2:245).

Look at what the lender receives. **First**, multiplication — *He will double it for you*. **Second**, and this is the part no ordinary loan carries: *and He will forgive you*. Ibn Kathir explains this as: He will erase your mistakes. So the return on this loan is paid in two currencies — increase in what you gave, and erasure of what you did wrong.

**Two names seal the offer.** *"And Allah is **Shakur**, **Halim**."* Ibn Kathir explains **Shakur** as: He gives abundantly in return for what was little. And **Halim** as: He forgives, pardons, covers and absolves the sins, mistakes, errors and shortcomings. Place those two names beside the human situation of this passage — a person who gives a small amount and whose record is full of failures — and you see why they were chosen. Shakur meets the smallness of your gift; Halim meets the size of your faults.

## Ayah 18: the seal

The surah ends: *"All-Knower of the unseen and the seen, the Almighty (al-'Aziz), the All-Wise (al-Hakim)."* Ibn Kathir notes that the explanation of these names has already preceded several times, and with that the tafsir of Surat At-Taghabun closes.

As a seal on this passage it reads with exactness. *Knower of the unseen and the seen* — He knows the charity no one saw, and the private motive behind the charity everyone saw; He knows which family pressure you resisted in silence. *Al-'Aziz*, the Almighty — nothing can stand between Him and the return He has promised. *Al-Hakim*, the All-Wise — the very test placed in your home was placed there wisely, and the great reward waits with Him for its Day.

## Living it

- Keep the warning of ayah 14 pointed where Ibn Zayd pointed it: *guard your religion*. The question is not "is my family difficult?" but "is my obedience to Allah quietly bending around them?"
- When they do pull you wrong, the ayah's own answer is pardon, overlooking and forgiveness — and the ruling Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records tells you it is not appropriate to give up on them totally, to be hostile, or to hate or curse them.
- Take ayah 15 as a diagnosis rather than a verdict. Love them the way the Prophet ﷺ loved al-Hasan and Husayn — openly, warmly, and with your eyes open to what that love can cost.
- Take ayah 16 as relief and demand together: you are asked for taqwa *as far as you are able* — a mercy if you are struggling, and a challenge if you have been coasting.
- Take ayah 17 literally. Every act of giving is filed as a loan with a Borrower who is neither unjust nor poor, who returns it multiplied and erases your mistakes on top.
